# Why Compare Means? {#sec-why-compare-means}

## Eight points {#sec-eight-points}

Twenty students sat a statistics exam, marked out of 100. Ten of them are in
Group A and ten are in Group B.

```{python}
#| label: setup
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(68)

N_PER_GROUP = 10
POPULATION_SIZE = 10_000

population = np.clip(np.round(rng.normal(70, 12, POPULATION_SIZE)), 0, 100)
group_a = rng.choice(population, N_PER_GROUP, replace=False)
group_b = rng.choice(population, N_PER_GROUP, replace=False)

print("Group A:", np.sort(group_a).astype(int))
print("Group B:", np.sort(group_b).astype(int))
print(f"\nAverages: {group_a.mean():.1f} and {group_b.mean():.1f}")
print(f"Gap:      {group_b.mean() - group_a.mean():.1f} points")
```

Eight points. Group B did better.

Notice that no individual student supports that claim. Group B contains the
lowest mark on the page, Group A contains a mark in the eighties, and the two
sets of scores sit on top of each other almost everywhere. Compare students one
by one and there is nothing to say. The eight points only exists once each group
is squeezed down to a single number, which is why the average is where we start.

So what does eight points mean?

## What chance produces {#sec-what-chance-produces}

To judge a gap we need something to judge it against, and the obvious candidate
is the gap we would have seen with no effect at all. If two groups of ten
routinely land eight points apart for no reason, our result is nothing. If they
almost never do, it is something.

Answering that means asking where these twenty students came from. They were
drawn from a year group of ten thousand, all of whom sat the exam. The year
averages 70, and most students land within about 12 points either side of it,
which is what it means to say the marks have a standard deviation of 12.

That population is the thing that lets us repeat the experiment. Draw ten
students, draw ten more, record the gap between their averages, and do it ten
thousand times. Every one of those gaps comes from a world with no effect in it,
because both groups were pulled from the same year the whole way through.

```{python}
#| label: null-distribution
def sample_gaps(students, n_sims=10_000, n=N_PER_GROUP):
    """Draw two groups, record the gap, repeat."""
    picked = np.array([rng.choice(students.size, 2 * n, replace=False)
                       for _ in range(n_sims)])
    marks = students[picked]
    return marks[:, n:].mean(axis=1) - marks[:, :n].mean(axis=1)

gaps = sample_gaps(population)

print(f"Average gap:       {gaps.mean():6.2f}")
print(f"Typical size:      {np.abs(gaps).mean():6.2f}")
print(f"Middle 95% within  {np.quantile(gaps, 0.025):.1f}"
      f" to {np.quantile(gaps, 0.975):.1f}")
print(f"Gap of 8 or more:  {np.mean(np.abs(gaps) >= 8):6.2%} of draws")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-null-distribution
#| fig-cap: "Gaps between two groups of ten, across 10,000 draws from the same year group. Both groups come from one population every time, so the true gap is always zero. The observed eight points is marked in red."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.hist(gaps, bins=60, color="#adb5bd", edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.4)
ax.axvline(8, color="#c92a2a", linewidth=2)
ax.set_xlabel("Gap between the two group averages (points)")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of draws")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

The gaps center on zero, so the procedure is honest. Repeat it enough and it
recovers the truth, which is that there is no difference at all. But hardly any
single draw lands on zero. Two groups of ten sit about four points apart as a
matter of course, the middle 95% runs past ten points in each direction, and
eight points or more turns up in roughly one draw out of seven.

Our eight points is sitting inside the ordinary range. It is not a finding. It is
what this procedure does when nothing is going on.

::: {.callout-note}
## "No difference" is a claim about the population

It does not mean two groups will come out with equal averages. They never do. It
means both groups were drawn from the same population, so their gap averages to
zero over many repetitions while any single gap does not.
:::

## The same eight points, twice {#sec-same-gap-twice}

Those numbers describe this exam, not exams in general. Change the exam and they
change with it.

Suppose the test is replaced with a much longer one, where a lucky guess moves a
mark far less and students end up closer together. The same ten thousand
students sit it, the year still averages 70, but the spread falls from 12 points
to 5.

```{python}
#| label: fig-two-exams
#| fig-cap: "Gaps produced by drawing two groups of ten, under the original exam (left) and the longer one (right). The same eight points is ordinary on one exam and almost unreachable on the other."
fine_population = np.clip(np.round(rng.normal(70, 5, POPULATION_SIZE)), 0, 100)
fine_gaps = sample_gaps(fine_population)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, data, label in zip(axes, [gaps, fine_gaps],
                           ["Original exam (spread 12)",
                            "Longer exam (spread 5)"]):
    ax.hist(data, bins=60, color="#adb5bd", edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.4)
    ax.axvline(8, color="#c92a2a", linewidth=2)
    ax.set_title(label, fontsize=11)
    ax.set_xlabel("Gap produced by chance (points)")
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Number of draws")
plt.show()

print("A gap of 8 points or more happens...")
print(f"  on the original exam: {np.mean(np.abs(gaps) >= 8):6.2%} of draws")
print(f"  on the longer exam:   {np.mean(np.abs(fine_gaps) >= 8):6.2%} of draws")
```

The same eight points means two different things. On the left it is what chance
hands you about one time in seven. On the right it happened twice in ten thousand
attempts.

Nothing about the eight points changed. What changed was the company it keeps.

**A gap carries no meaning on its own. It acquires meaning only next to the gap
that chance produces anyway.**

Which leaves us one step short. We found the gaps chance produces by drawing ten
thousand times from a year group we could see in full, and no real study has
either of those. You get one draw, and the population stays hidden. The next
chapter is about how to do this anyway.
